metric_rationale: The experimental design consists of trials where Option A generally has a single high-validity cue in its favor, while Option B has multiple lower-validity cues. Take The Best (TTB) will consistently choose Option A across all trials because it stops at the first discriminating cue (which always favors A). In contrast, the Weighted Additive (WADD) model integrates all cues, and the coalition of multiple lower-validity cues for Option B will frequently outweigh Option A's single best cue. By computing the proportion of Option B choices (response == 1) specifically on trials where B has a greater number of positive cues than A, we perfectly isolate the compensatory nature of WADD from the non-compensatory nature of TTB. TTB's expected value will be near 0 (driven only by lapse noise), while WADD's will be significantly higher.

Calculates the proportion of trials where the participant's choice aligns with the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic. TTB models will exhibit a very high match rate (close to 1.0, modulo noise), whereas WADD models, being compensatory, will frequently choose the option favored by a coalition of lower-validity cues (e.g., choosing B when A has the single best cue but B has many good cues), resulting in a significantly lower match rate.

This metric isolates the critical trials where Tallying (Equal-Weight) and WADD make diametrically opposing predictions. It does so by computing both the unweighted sum of features and the validity-weighted sum, and filtering for trials where the two models favor different options. The metric computes the proportion of choices on these critical trials that align with the Tallying prediction. Data simulated under Tallying will yield a high proportion (close to 1.0, minus lapse rate), while data simulated under WADD will yield a low proportion (close to 0.0, plus lapse rate). By focusing exclusively on the trials that dissociate the theories, the metric maximizes the between-theory difference while minimizing within-theory variance.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices consistent with the Weighted Additive (WADD) theory on the critical trials where WADD and Tallying make diametrically opposed predictions. Specifically, it looks at trials where one option has fewer but higher-validity cues (e.g., [1, 1, 0, 0, 0]) and the other has more but lower-validity cues (e.g., [0, 0, 1, 1, 1]). WADD predicts a preference for the former, while Tallying predicts a preference for the latter. The metric will be close to 1 for WADD and close to 0 for Tallying.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Tallying strategy (choosing the option with the higher total number of positive features) strictly on trials where the two options have an unequal number of positive features. In the chosen experimental design, the trials with unequal feature sums are perfectly engineered so that the option with more features lacks the single most valid discriminating cue. As a result, Tallying and NV-TTB will make diametrically opposed predictions on these trials. Tallying will score very high on this metric, whereas NV-TTB will score very low.

This metric isolates 'discordant' trials where the two theories make strictly opposite predictions. Specifically, it looks for trials where one option has the highest-validity cue (favored by NV-TTB) but the other option has a strictly greater total number of positive cues (favored by Tallying). The metric returns the proportion of choices on these critical trials that align with the NV-TTB prediction. NV-TTB will produce a metric value close to 1, whereas Tallying will produce a metric value close to 0.

Focuses on trials where the simple sum of positive features is tied between options A and B, but the sum of objective validities differs. Pure Tallying ignores validities and predicts a 50/50 choice on these trials, making the proportion of choices for the higher-validity option approximately 0.5. Validity-Biased Tallying mixes uniform weighting with objective validities, so it will systematically prefer the higher-validity option, leading to a proportion significantly greater than 0.5.

In trials where both options have an equal number of positive features, pure Tallying predicts indifference (a 50/50 choice probability) because it ignores cue validities. Validity-Biased Tallying, however, still incorporates cue validities to some extent, leading to a systematic preference for the option with higher-validity features. In the chosen experimental design, all trials with tied feature counts (Trials 1, 3, 5, and 8) are constructed such that Option A has a higher sum of objective validities. Therefore, calculating the proportion of times Option A is chosen (response == 0) on these tied trials will strongly discriminate the two theories: Tallying predicts a value of ~0.5, whereas Validity-Biased Tallying predicts a value significantly greater than 0.5.
